Minkowski content and natural parameterization for the Schramm–Loewner evolution

DOI: 10.1214/13-AOP874Volume: 433

Abstract

We prove the existence and nontriviality of the dd-dimensional 4 Minkowski content for the Schramm–Loewner evolution (SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa}) with κ<8\kappa<8 and d=1+κ8d=1+\frac{\kappa}{8}. We show that this is a multiple of the natural parameterization.

Keywords: 
Schramm–Loewner evolution, Minkowski content, natural parameterization,

and

1 Introduction

A number of measures on paths or clusters on two-dimensional lattices arising from critical statistical mechanical models are believed to exhibit some kind of conformal invariance in the scaling limit. Schramm [13] introduced a one-parameter family of such processes, now called the (chordal) Schramm–Loewner evolution with parameter κ\kappa (SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa}) and showed that these give the only possible limits for conformally invariant processes in simply connected domains satisfying a certain “domain Markov property.” He defined the process as a probability measure on curves from 00 to ∞\infty in ℍ{\mathbb{H}} and then used conformal invariance to define the process in other simply connected domains.

The definition of the process in ℍ{\mathbb{H}} uses the half-plane Loewner equation. Suppose γ:(0,t]→ℍ¯\gamma\colon\;(0,t]\rightarrow\overline{{\mathbb{H}}} is a curve with γ⁡(0)=0\gamma(0)=0, and let γt=γ(0,t]\gamma_{t}=\gamma(0,t]. Let HtH_{t} denote the unbounded component of ℍ∖γt{\mathbb{H}}\setminus\gamma_{t}. We assume that γ\gamma is noncrossing in the sense that for all s<ts<t, γ[s,∞)⊂H¯s\gamma[s,\infty)\subset\overline{H}_{s}, and γ⁡[s,t]∩Hs\gamma[s,t]\cap H_{s} is nonempty. Let gt:Ht→ℍg_{t}\colon\;H_{t}\rightarrow{\mathbb{H}} be the unique conformal transformation with gt​(z)−z=o⁡(1)g_{t}(z)-z=o(1) as z→∞z\rightarrow\infty. Then for every a>0a>0, there exists a reparameterization of the curve such that the following holds:

  • •

    For z∈ℍz\in{\mathbb{H}}, the map t↦gt​(z)t\mapsto g_{t}(z) is a smooth flow and satisfies the Loewner differential equation

    ∂tgt​(z)=agt​(z)−Ut,g0​(z)=z,\partial_{t}g_{t}(z)=\frac{a}{g_{t}(z)-U_{t}},\qquad g_{0}(z)=z,

    where UtU_{t} is a continuous function on ℝ{\mathbb{R}}. This equation is valid up to a time Tz∈(0,∞]T_{z}\in(0,\infty].

Under the reparameterization, the transformation gtg_{t} satisfies

gt​(z)=z+a​tz+O⁡(|z|−2),z→∞.g_{t}(z)=z+\frac{at}{z}+O\bigl(|z|^{-2}\bigr),\qquad z\rightarrow\infty.

We say that the curve is parameterized by (half-plane) capacity. Schramm-defined chordal SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} to be the solution to the Loewner equation with a=2a=2 and UtU_{t} a Brownian motion with variance parameter κ\kappa. An equivalent definition (up to a linear time change) is to choose UtU_{t} to be a standard Brownian motion and a=2/κa=2/\kappa. It has been shown that a number of discrete random models have SLE\mathrm{SLE} as the scaling limit provided that the discrete models are parameterized using (half-plane) capacity. Examples are loop-erased random walk for κ=2\kappa=2 [7], Ising interfaces for κ=3\kappa=3 [16], harmonic explorer for κ=4\kappa=4 [14], percolation interfaces on the triangular lattice for κ=6\kappa=6 [15] and uniform spanning trees for κ=8\kappa=8 [7].

If DD is a simply connected domain with distinct boundary points w1,w2w_{1},w_{2} where ∂D\partial D is nice in neighborhoods of w1,w2w_{1},w_{2}, then chordal SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} from w1w_{1} to w2w_{2} in DD is defined by taking the conformal image of SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} in the upper half plane under a transformation F:ℍ→DF\colon\;{\mathbb{H}}\rightarrow D with F⁡(0)=w1,F⁡(∞)=w2F(0)=w_{1},F(\infty)=w_{2}. The map FF is not unique, but scale invariance of SLE\mathrm{SLE} in ℍ{\mathbb{H}} shows that the distribution on paths is independent of the choice. This can be considered as a measure on the curves F∘γF\circ\gamma with the induced parameterization or as a measure on curves modulo reparameterization.

While the capacity parameterization is useful for analyzing the curve, it is not the scaling limit of the “natural” parameterization of the discrete models. For example, for loop-erased walks, it is natural to parameterize by the length of the random walk. One can ask whether the curves parameterized by a normalized version of this “natural length” converge to SLE\mathrm{SLE} with a different parameterization. The Hausdorff dimension of the SLE\mathrm{SLE} paths [2] is d=1+min⁡{κ8,1}d=1+\min\{\frac{\kappa}{8},1\}. It was conjectured in [8] that the “natural length” of an SLE\mathrm{SLE} path might be given by the dd-dimensional Minkowski content defined as follows. Let

Contd⁡(γt;r)=er⁡(2−d)​Area⁡{z:dist⁡(z,γt)≤e−r}.{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(\gamma_{t};r)=e^{r(2-d)}{\operatorname{Area}}\bigl\{z\colon\;\operatorname{dist}(z,\gamma_{t})\leq e^{-r}\bigr\}.

Then the dd-dimensional content is

Contd⁡(γt)=limr→∞Contd⁡(γt;r),{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(\gamma_{t})=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(\gamma_{t};r),

provided that the limit exists. If κ≥8\kappa\geq 8, then d=2d=2, and the two-dimensional Minkowski content is the same as the area and the limit clearly exists. If κ<8\kappa<8, it is not at all obvious that the limit exists and is positive for t>0t>0. The main goal of this paper is to prove this.

Before stating the theorem, we will set some notational conventions for this paper. Let 0<κ<80<\kappa<8 and let

a=2κ∈(1/4,∞),d=1+κ8=1+14​a∈(1,2).a=\frac{2}{\kappa}\in(1/4,\infty),\qquad d=1+\frac{\kappa}{8}=1+\frac{1}{4a}\in(1,2).

Recall that γt=γ(0,t]\gamma_{t}=\gamma(0,t] and we write γ=γ∞=γ⁡(0,∞)\gamma=\gamma_{\infty}=\gamma(0,\infty) for the entire path of the curve. The Green’s function for κ<8\kappa<8 is defined by

G(z)=limr→∞er⁡(2−d)ℙ{dist(z,γ)≤e−r}.G(z)=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}e^{r(2-d)}{\mathbb{P}}\bigl\{\operatorname{dist}(z,\gamma)\leq e^{-r}\bigr\}.

This limit exists (see Section 2.3) and there exists c=cκc=c_{\kappa} such that

G⁡(z)=c​[ℑ⁡z]d−2​[sin⁡arg⁡z]4​a−1.G(z)=c[\Im z]^{d-2}[\sin\arg z]^{4a-1}.

Our definition of the Green’s function differs by a multiplicative constant from that in other papers. If F:D→ℍF\colon\;D\rightarrow{\mathbb{H}} is a conformal transformation with F⁡(w1)=0F(w_{1})=0, F⁡(w2)=∞F(w_{2})=\infty, we define

GD​(z,w1,w2)=|F′​(z)|2−d​G​(F⁡(z)).G_{D}(z;w_{1},w_{2})=\bigl|F^{\prime}(z)\bigr|^{2-d}G\bigl(F(z)\bigr).

There is also a two-point Green’s function (see Section 2.4)

G⁡(z,w)=limr→∞e2​r​(2−d)​ℙ​{dist⁡(z,γ)≤e−r,dist⁡(w,γ)≤e−r}.G(z,w)=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}e^{2r(2-d)}{\mathbb{P}}\bigl\{\operatorname{dist}(z,\gamma)\leq e^{-r},\operatorname{dist}(w,\gamma)\leq e^{-r}\bigr\}.

If D⊂ℍD\subset{\mathbb{H}}, let

G⁡(D)=∫DG⁡(z)​𝑑A​(z),G2​(D)=∫D∫DG⁡(z,w)​𝑑A​(z)​𝑑A​(w),G(D)=\int_{D}G(z)\,dA(z),\qquad G^{2}(D)=\int_{D}\int_{D}G(z,w)\,dA(z)\,dA(w),

where d​AdA denotes integration with respect to area. We call γ⁡(t)\gamma(t) a double point for the SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} path if there exists s<ts<t such that γ⁡(t)∈∂Hs\gamma(t)\in\partial H_{s}. If 0<κ≤40<\kappa\leq 4, the SLE\mathrm{SLE} path has no double points while they exist for 4<κ<84<\kappa<8.

Theorem 1.1

If 0<κ<80<\kappa<8 there exists β>0\beta>0, such that if γ⁡(t)\gamma(t) is an SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} curve from 00 to ∞\infty in ℍ{\mathbb{H}} parameterized by capacity, then with probability one, the following holds:

  • •

    For every t>0t>0, the Minkowski content

    Θt=Contd⁡(γt)=limr→∞Contd⁡(γt;r),\Theta_{t}={\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(\gamma_{t})=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(\gamma_{t};r),

    exists.

  • •

    The function t↦Θtt\mapsto\Theta_{t} is strictly increasing and if s<ts<t,

    Θt−Θs=Contd(γ[s,t])=Contd(γ(s,t]∩Hs).\Theta_{t}-\Theta_{s}={\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}\bigl(\gamma[s,t]\bigr)={\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}\bigl(\gamma(s,t]\cap H_{s}\bigr).
  • •

    On every bounded interval [0,t0][0,t_{0}], Θt\Theta_{t} is Hölder continuous of order β\beta.

Moreover, if D⊂ℍD\subset{\mathbb{H}} is a bounded domain with piecewise smooth boundary, then

𝔼⁡[Contd⁡(γ∩D)]\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\bigl[{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(\gamma\cap D)\bigr] =\displaystyle= G⁡(D),\displaystyle G(D),
𝔼⁡[Contd⁡(γ∩D)2]\displaystyle{\mathbb{E}}\bigl[{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(\gamma\cap D)^{2}\bigr] =\displaystyle= G2​(D),\displaystyle G^{2}(D),

and if t>0t>0,

𝔼⁡[Contd⁡(γ∩D)|γt]=Contd⁡(γt∩D)+∫DGHt​(z,γ⁡(t),∞)​𝑑A​(z).{\mathbb{E}}\bigl[{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(\gamma\cap D)|\gamma_{t}\bigr]={\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(\gamma_{t}\cap D)+\int_{D}G_{H_{t}}\bigl(z;\gamma(t),\infty\bigr)\,dA(z).

The proof will show that we can choose any β<α0​d/2\beta<\alpha_{0}d/2 where

β<d2​min⁡{1−κ24+2​κ−8​8+κ,12}>0.\beta<\frac{d}{2}\min\biggl\{1-\frac{\kappa}{24+2\kappa-8\sqrt{8+\kappa}},\frac{1}{2}\biggr\}>0.

The theorem allows us to define SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} with the natural parameterization by letting

γ~​(t)=γ⁡(σt),σt=inf{s:Θs=t}.\tilde{\gamma}(t)=\gamma(\sigma_{t}),\qquad\sigma_{t}=\inf\{s\colon\;\Theta_{s}=t\}.

Under this parameterization with probability one for all tt,

Contd⁡(γ~t)=t.{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(\tilde{\gamma}_{t})=t.

If F:ℍ→DF\colon\;{\mathbb{H}}\rightarrow D with F⁡(0)=w1,F⁡(∞)=w2F(0)=w_{1},F(\infty)=w_{2} is a conformal transformation, then as in [4] the natural parameterization in DD can be defined by saying that the time to traverse F​(γ~​[s,t])F(\tilde{\gamma}[s,t]) is

∫st|F′​(γ~​(r))|d​𝑑r.\int_{s}^{t}\bigl|F^{\prime}\bigl(\tilde{\gamma}(r)\bigr)\bigr|^{d}\,dr. (1)

If γ~​[s,t]⊂ℍ\tilde{\gamma}[s,t]\subset{\mathbb{H}}, we can see that this is the same as Contd⁡[F∘γ~​[s,t]]{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}[F\circ\tilde{\gamma}[s,t]]. We expect this to be true for all nice DD. The only question is the intersection of the curve with the boundary for 4<κ<84<\kappa<8 with DD having a nonsmooth boundary, perhaps of large dimension.

As an example, let DD be the unit disk 𝔻{\mathbb{D}} and let w1=1,w2=−1w_{1}=1,w_{2}=-1. In this case, the map F:ℍ→𝔻F\colon\;{\mathbb{H}}\rightarrow{\mathbb{D}} extends analytically to ℝ{\mathbb{R}} and there is no problem establishing that (1) equals Contd⁡[F∘γ~​[s,t]]{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}[F\circ\tilde{\gamma}[s,t]]. Let γ⁡(t)\gamma(t) be the SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} path in ℍ{\mathbb{H}} with the capacity parameterization, and let η​(t)=F​(γ~​(t))\eta(t)=F(\tilde{\gamma}(t)) which is an SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} curve from 11 to −1-1 in 𝔻{\mathbb{D}}. Let Θt=Contd⁡[ηt]\Theta_{t}={\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}[\eta_{t}]. In this case, Θ∞\Theta_{\infty} is an integrable random variable with

𝔼⁡[Θ∞]=∫𝔻G𝔻​(z,1,−1)​𝑑A​(z)<∞.{\mathbb{E}}[\Theta_{\infty}]=\int_{\mathbb{D}}G_{\mathbb{D}}(z;1,-1)\,dA(z)<\infty.

Moreover,

𝔼⁡[Θ∞|ηt]=Θt+Ψt,{\mathbb{E}}[\Theta_{\infty}|\eta_{t}]=\Theta_{t}+\Psi_{t},

where

Ψt=∫DtGDt​(z,η⁡(t),−1)​𝑑A​(z).\Psi_{t}=\int_{D_{t}}G_{D_{t}}\bigl(z;\eta(t),-1\bigr)\,dA(z).

Since Mt:=𝔼⁡[Θ∞|ηt]M_{t}:={\mathbb{E}}[\Theta_{\infty}|\eta_{t}] is a martingale, we can see that Θt\Theta_{t} is the unique increasing process such that Ψt+Θt\Psi_{t}+\Theta_{t} is a martingale. This is a Doob–Meyer decomposition.

In [8], the natural parameterization was defined to be the unique process Θt\Theta_{t} which makes Ψt+Θt\Psi_{t}+\Theta_{t} a martingale. While this is a simple definition, it requires moment bounds in order to make sure that the process exists (uniqueness is easy). Indeed, it is not hard to see that Mt​(z):=GDt​(z,η⁡(t),−1)M_{t}(z):=G_{D_{t}}(z;\eta(t),-1) is a local martingale, and hence Ψt\Psi_{t} is an integral of positive local martingales. If Ψt\Psi_{t} were also a local martingale, then no nontrivial Θt\Theta_{t} could exist.

  • •

    In [8], it was shown that for κ<5.0,…,\kappa<5.0,\ldots, the process Θt\Theta_{t} exists in ℍ{\mathbb{H}} (the definition has to be modified slightly in ℍ{\mathbb{H}} because Ψ0\Psi_{0} as we have defined it above is infinite—this is not very difficult). The necessary second moment bounds were obtained using the reverse Loewner flow. It was shown that for this range of κ\kappa, there exists α0=α0​(κ)>0\alpha_{0}=\alpha_{0}(\kappa)>0 such that the function t↦Θtt\mapsto\Theta_{t} is Hölder continuous of order α\alpha for α<α0\alpha<\alpha_{0}.

  • •

    In [10], the natural parameterization was shown to exist for all κ<8\kappa<8. There the necessary two-point estimates were obtained from estimates on the two-point Green’s function [2, 9]. However, the estimates were not strong enough to determine Hölder continuity of the function Θt\Theta_{t}.

  • •

    In [4], a new proof was given for all κ<8\kappa<8 combining ideas in [8, 10] with known results about the Hölder continuity of the Schramm–Loewner evolution (with respect to the capacity parameterization). This established continuity and Hölder continuity of the natural parameterization for all κ\kappa.

Let us discuss some conclusions that we can derive. If Θt=Contd⁡(γt)\Theta_{t}={\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(\gamma_{t}), then clearly Θt\Theta_{t} is increasing and measurable with respect to γt\gamma_{t}. The conditional distribution of Contd⁡[γ⁡(t,∞)]{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}[\gamma(t,\infty)] given γt\gamma_{t} is the same as the distribution of the Minkowski content for SLE\mathrm{SLE} from γ⁡(t)\gamma(t) to −1-1 in DtD_{t}. In particular, using the fact that Θt−Θs=Contd(γ(s,t]∩Ds)\Theta_{t}-\Theta_{s}={\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(\gamma(s,t]\cap D_{s}), we have

𝔼⁡[Θ∞−Θt|γt]=∫DtG^t​(z)​𝑑A​(z),{\mathbb{E}}[\Theta_{\infty}-\Theta_{t}|\gamma_{t}]=\int_{D_{t}}{\widehat{G}}_{t}(z)\,dA(z),

where G^t​(z)=GDt​(z,γ⁡(t),−1){\widehat{G}}_{t}(z)=G_{D_{t}}(z;\gamma(t),-1). Therefore,

Θt+∫DtG^t​(z)​𝑑A​(z)\Theta_{t}+\int_{D_{t}}{\widehat{G}}_{t}(z)\,dA(z)

is a martingale. Uniqueness of the Doob–Meyer decomposition shows that our Θt\Theta_{t} must be the same as the natural parameterization as discussed in [8, 10, 4]. Using the Minkowski content as the definition, we immediately get independence of domain as well as reversibility of the natural parameterization, that is, the time to traverse γ⁡[s,t]\gamma[s,t] is the same as the time to traverse the path in the reverse direction. By independence of domain, we mean that if γ\gamma is an SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} curve in ℍ{\mathbb{H}} and D⊂ℍD\subset{\mathbb{H}} with γ⁡(0,∞)⊂D\gamma(0,\infty)\subset D, then the natural parameterization for γ\gamma considered as an SLE\mathrm{SLE} curve in DD is the same as that for the SLE\mathrm{SLE} curve in ℍ{\mathbb{H}}. While this is clearly a property that we would expect from a “natural” parameterization, it is not at all obvious using the definition in [8].

Another possible candidate for the “natural length” of an SLE\mathrm{SLE} curve might be the dd-dimensional Hausdorff measure. However, it has been proved [12] that this is zero with probability one. It is unknown whether one can find a Hausdorff measure with a different gauge function which would give a nontrivial quantity.

1.1 Outline of the paper

Section 2 sets notation for the paper and reviews previous work. We define the Minkowski content in Section 2.2 and derive some simple properties. The Green’s function for chordal SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} is reviewed in Section 2.3. This is a normalized limit of the probability of getting near a point zz. We also discuss estimates in [9] concerning the probability that an SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} path gets close to two points. In the following subsection, we discuss some of the ideas used to prove two-point estimates; in particular, some precise formulations are made of the rough statement “after an SLE curve gets close to zz it is unlikely to get close again.” This section uses ideas from [6, 9].

The proof of the main result is in the remainder of the paper. Before going into specifics, let us outline the basic idea of the proof. For ease, let us fix a square, say Γ=[0,1)+i[1,2)\Gamma=[0,1)+i[1,2) and consider γ∩Γ\gamma\cap\Gamma. For each z∈Γz\in\Gamma and r>0r>0, let τr​(z)=inf{t:|γ⁡(t)−z|≤e−r}\tau_{r}(z)=\inf\{t\colon\;|\gamma(t)-z|\leq e^{-r}\} and let Jr​(z)J_{r}(z) be er⁡(2−d)e^{r(2-d)} times the indicator function of the event {τr(z)<∞}\{\tau_{r}(z)<\infty\}. Let Tr​(z)T_{r}(z) be the first time that the conformal radius of zz in ℍ∖γ(0,t]{\mathbb{H}}\setminus\gamma(0,t] equals e−r+2e^{-r+2}. The Koebe (1/4)(1/4)-theorem implies that Tr​(z)<τr​(z)T_{r}(z)<\tau_{r}(z). By comparison with “two-sided radial” (SLE\mathrm{SLE} conditioned to go through zz), one can show that there exists c1c_{1} such that ℙ{Tr(z)<∞}∼c1G(z)er⁡(d−2){\mathbb{P}}\{T_{r}(z)<\infty\}\sim c_{1}G(z)e^{r(d-2)}. If rr is large, and we view the path γ​[0,Tr​(z)]\gamma[0,T_{r}(z)] near zz, then locally it appears like a path with the distribution of two-sided radial SLE\mathrm{SLE}. Using this, one can see that

ℙ⁡{Jr​(z)>0|Tr​(z)<∞}=ρ+o⁡(1),r→∞,{\mathbb{P}}\bigl\{J_{r}(z)>0|T_{r}(z)<\infty\bigr\}=\rho+o(1),\qquad r\rightarrow\infty,

where ρ\rho is independent of zz, and using this in turn, we get a one-point estimate

𝔼⁡[Jr​(z)]=c1​ρ​G​(z)+o⁡(1).{\mathbb{E}}\bigl[J_{r}(z)\bigr]=c_{1}\rho G(z)+o(1). (2)

If we fix δ>0\delta>0, we can see similarly that there exists ρ′\rho^{\prime} such that

ℙ⁡{Jr+δ​(z)>0|Tr​(z)<∞}=ρ′+o⁡(1),r→∞,{\mathbb{P}}\bigl\{J_{r+\delta}(z)>0|T_{r}(z)<\infty\bigr\}=\rho^{\prime}+o(1),\qquad r\rightarrow\infty,

and by using (2), we see that ρ′=eδ⁡(d−2)​ρ\rho^{\prime}=e^{\delta(d-2)}\rho. In other words, 𝔼⁡[Jr+δ​(z)−Jr​(z)]=o⁡(1){\mathbb{E}}[J_{r+\delta}(z)-J_{r}(z)]=o(1). The conditional distribution of Jr+δ​(z)−Jr​(z)J_{r+\delta}(z)-J_{r}(z) given γ​[0,Tr​(z)]\gamma[0,T_{r}(z)] is determined (up to a small error) by the way the curve γ\gamma looks near γ​(Tr​(z))\gamma(T_{r}(z)), and this latter distribution is understood through two-sided radial SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa}. If z,wz,w are not very close together and the SLE\mathrm{SLE} curve gets close to both zz and ww, we might hope (and, indeed, this is what we show) that the local behavior of γ\gamma near γ​(Tr​(z))\gamma(T_{r}(z)) and near γ​(Tr​(w))\gamma(T_{r}(w)) are almost independent. The upshot of this is that if we consider the random variable

Yr=∫Γ[Jr+δ​(z)−Jr​(z)]​𝑑A​(z),Y_{r}=\int_{\Gamma}\bigl[J_{r+\delta}(z)-J_{r}(z)\bigr]\,dA(z),

then 𝔼⁡[Yr2]{\mathbb{E}}[Y_{r}^{2}] is small. We show that 𝔼⁡[Yr2]≤c​e−β​r{\mathbb{E}}[Y_{r}^{2}]\leq ce^{-\beta r}, from which we conclude that

limr→∞∫ΓJr​(z)​𝑑A​(z)\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}\int_{\Gamma}J_{r}(z)\,dA(z)

exists as a limit in L2L^{2} and with probability one.

This outline is carried out in Section 3.1 assuming a moment bound, Theorem 3.2 which is proved later. This establishes that with probability one Contd⁡[γ∩Γ]{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}[\gamma\cap\Gamma] exists for every dyadic square Γ\Gamma. Section 3.2 uses this to prove the statements in Theorem 1.1, again leaving one fact for the last section.

The main estimates are proved in the final section. Section 4.2 analyzes the one-point estimate, that is, the estimate for getting close to a single point zz. See Theorem 4.2. A key to the two-point estimate is to understand the one-point estimate very well. For ease, we consider SLE\mathrm{SLE} in the disk between boundary points and choose the origin to be the target point. Two-sided radial, which is an example of what are sometimes called SLE⁡(κ,ρ)\mathrm{SLE}(\kappa,\rho) processes, describes chordal SLE\mathrm{SLE} “conditioned to go through zz.” It can be analyzed by a one-dimensional SDE. We use this to study SLE\mathrm{SLE} conditioned to get near zz. To do the two-point estimate, we start in Section 2.4 by reviewing the basic idea that after one gets close to a point, one tends not to return to it. This statement requires care to make precise. See Lemmas 2.5 and 2.6. In the final section, we complete the proof giving a rigorous version of the rough outline above.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 Notations and distortion

We fix κ<8\kappa<8 and allow all constants to depend implicitly on κ\kappa. Recall that a=2/κa=2/\kappa and d=1+κ8d=1+\frac{\kappa}{8}. If γ\gamma is an SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} curve from w1w_{1} to w2w_{2} in a simply connected domain DD, we write γt=γ(0,t]={γ(s): 0<s≤t}\gamma_{t}=\gamma(0,t]=\{\gamma(s)\colon\;0<s\leq t\}.

If n,j,kn,j,k are integers, we write Γn​(j,k)\Gamma_{n}(j,k) for the dyadic square

Γn(j,k)=[j2−n,(j+1)2−n)×i[k2−n,(k+1)2−n).\Gamma_{n}(j,k)=\bigl[j2^{-n},(j+1)2^{-n}\bigr)\times i\bigl[k2^{-n},(k+1)2^{-n}\bigr).

Let

2.2 Minkowski content

The dd-dimensional Minkowski content is one way to “measure” the size of a dd-dimensional fractal. We use the quotes because the content is not technically a measure. Its definition is in some ways more natural than dd-dimensional Hausdorff measure; however, it has the disadvantage that it is defined in terms of a limit that does not always exist. We will restrict our consideration to 1<d<21<d<2 and V⊂ℂV\subset{\mathbb{C}}.

Let

Contd⁡(V,r)\displaystyle{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(V;r) =\displaystyle= er⁡(2−d)​Area⁡{z:dist⁡(z,V)≤e−r}\displaystyle e^{r(2-d)}\operatorname{Area}\bigl\{z\colon\;\operatorname{dist}(z,V)\leq e^{-r}\bigr\}
=\displaystyle= er⁡(2−d)∫ℂ1{dist(z,V)≤e−r}dA(z).\displaystyle e^{r(2-d)}\int_{\mathbb{C}}1\bigl\{\operatorname{dist}(z,V)\leq e^{-r}\bigr\}\,dA(z).

Here, and throughout this paper, d​AdA denotes integration with respect to two-dimensional Lebesgue measure. The upper and lower dd-dimensional Minkowski contents are defined by

Contd+⁡(V;r)\displaystyle{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}^{+}}(V;r) =\displaystyle= sups≥rContd⁡(V;s),Contd+⁡(V)=limr→∞Contd+⁡(V;r),\displaystyle\sup_{s\geq r}{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(V;s),\qquad{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}^{+}}(V)=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}^{+}}(V;r),
Contd−⁡(V;r)\displaystyle{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}^{-}}(V;r) =\displaystyle= infs≥rContd⁡(V;s),Contd−⁡(V)=limr→∞Contd−⁡(V;r).\displaystyle\inf_{s\geq r}{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(V;s),\qquad{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}^{-}}(V)=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}^{-}}(V;r).

The dd-dimensional Minkowski content is defined if Contd+⁡(V)=Contd−⁡(V){\operatorname{Cont}_{d}^{+}}(V)={\operatorname{Cont}_{d}^{-}}(V) in which case

Contd⁡(V)=limr→∞Contd⁡(V;r).{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(V)=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(V;r).

The following simple lemma lists the basic properties of Minkowski content that we will use.

Lemma 2.2

  • •

    If Contd⁡(V),Contd⁡(V′){\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(V),{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(V^{\prime}) exist and dist⁡(V,V′)>0\operatorname{dist}(V,V^{\prime})>0, then Contd⁡(V∪V′){\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(V\cup V^{\prime}) exists and

    Contd⁡(V∪V′)=Contd⁡(V)+Contd⁡(V′).{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}\bigl(V\cup V^{\prime}\bigr)={\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(V)+{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}\bigl(V^{\prime}\bigr).

  • •

    Contd(V)=limr→∞er⁡(2−d)∫D1{dist(z,V)≤e−r}dA(z),{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(V)=\lim_{r\rightarrow\infty}e^{r(2-d)}\int_{D}1\bigl\{\operatorname{dist}(z,V)\leq e^{-r}\bigr\}\,dA(z), (3)

    provided that either side exists.

  • •

    Suppose V1,V2,…V_{1},V_{2},\ldots are bounded sets for which Contd⁡(Vn){\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(V_{n}) is well defined. Let VV be a bounded set such that

    limn→∞[Contd+⁡(V∖Vn)+Contd+⁡(Vn∖V)]=0.\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\bigl[{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}^{+}}(V\setminus V_{n})+{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}^{+}}(V_{n}\setminus V)\bigr]=0.

2.4 Two-point estimates

A basic principle in proving two-point estimates for SLE\mathrm{SLE} is the idea that if a path gets very close to a point zz and then gets away from zz, then it is unlikely to get even closer to zz. While this is the heuristic, as just stated the principle is not always valid. Since this idea is important in several of our proofs, we will spend some time to formulate and prove a precise version. We are expanding on ideas in [6, 4]. Let γ\gamma be an SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} curve from 00 to ∞\infty in ℍ{\mathbb{H}}. As before, if z∈ℍz\in{\mathbb{H}}, let

τr​(z)=inf{t:|γ⁡(t)−z|=e−r}.\tau_{r}(z)=\inf\bigl\{t\colon\;\bigl|\gamma(t)-z\bigr|=e^{-r}\bigr\}.

If τr=τr​(z)<∞\tau_{r}=\tau_{r}(z)<\infty, let H=HτrH=H_{\tau_{r}} denote the unbounded component of ℍ∖γτr{\mathbb{H}}\setminus\gamma_{\tau_{r}}, let ℬu=ℬu​(r,z){\mathcal{B}}_{u}={\mathcal{B}}_{u}(r,z) denote the disk of radius e−u​re^{-ur} containing zz, and let ℬ=ℬ1{\mathcal{B}}={\mathcal{B}}_{1} denote the disk of radius e−re^{-r} about zz. Let Vu=Vu​(r,z)V_{u}=V_{u}(r,z) denote the connected component of ℬu∩H{\mathcal{B}}_{u}\cap H containing zz. If u≤1u\leq 1, the intersection of ∂Vu\partial V_{u} with HH is a disjoint union of open arcs in ∂ℬu\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{u} each of whose endpoints is in ∂H\partial H. There is a unique such arc ll, that we denote by lu=lu​(r,z)l_{u}=l_{u}(r,z), such that zz is contained in the bounded component of H∖lH\setminus l. Simple connectedness of HH is used to see that this arc is unique. However, one may note the following facts:

  • •

    The bounded component of H∖luH\setminus l_{u} does not need to be contained in ℬu{\mathcal{B}}_{u}. Indeed, we have no universal bound on the diameter of the bounded component.

  • •

    There may be other subarcs ll of ∂ℬu∩H\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{u}\cap H such that zz is in the bounded component of H∖lH\setminus l. However, these arcs are not on ∂Vu\partial V_{u}.

For 0<u≤10<u\leq 1, let

σ=σu​(r,z)=inf{t≥τr:γ⁡(t)∈lu¯}.\sigma=\sigma_{u}(r,z)=\inf\bigl\{t\geq\tau_{r}\colon\;\gamma(t)\in\overline{l_{u}}\bigr\}.

Then a correct, although still imprecise, version of our heuristic principle is: if τr<∞\tau_{r}<\infty, then after time σ\sigma the path is unlikely to get closer to zz. We will now be more precise. Note that for fixed z,u,rz,u,r, with probability one γ⁡(σ)∈lu\gamma(\sigma)\in l_{u}. In this case (which we now assume), lu∖{γ⁡(σ)}l_{u}\setminus\{\gamma(\sigma)\} consists of two crosscuts of HσH_{\sigma} that we denote by lu∗l^{*}_{u} and lu∗⁣∗l^{**}_{u}. If z∈Hσz\in H_{\sigma}, which is always true if κ≤4\kappa\leq 4, we let lu∗l^{*}_{u} be the crosscut such that zz lies in the bounded component of Hσ∖lu∗H_{\sigma}\setminus l^{*}_{u}. If τr<∞\tau_{r}<\infty, define λ=λ⁡(r,z,u)≥1\lambda=\lambda(r,z,u)\geq 1 by

dist⁡[z,γσ]=e−λ​r.\operatorname{dist}[z,\gamma_{\sigma}]=e^{-\lambda r}.

Let lλ∗l_{\lambda}^{*} denote the connected subarc of ∂ℬλ∩Hσ\partial{\mathcal{B}}_{\lambda}\cap H_{\sigma} that separates zz from infinity. (If the intersection of γσ\gamma_{\sigma} with ℬλ{\mathcal{B}}_{\lambda} is a single point, which we expect to be the case with probability one, then lλ∗l_{\lambda}^{*} is a circle with a single point deleted.) See Figure 1 for a figure showing illustrating these quantities.

Since we will use it in several proofs, we recall that if DD is a domain and η1,η2\eta^{1},\eta^{2} are disjoint subarcs of ∂D\partial D, then the (Brownian) excursion measure between η1,η2\eta^{1},\eta^{2} is given by

ℰD​(η1,η2)=∫η1∂nϕ⁡(z)​|𝑑z|,{\mathcal{E}}_{D}\bigl(\eta^{1},\eta^{2}\bigr)=\int_{\eta^{1}}\partial_{n}\phi(z)|dz|,

where ∂n\partial_{n} denotes the inward normal derivative and ϕ=ϕD,η2\phi=\phi_{D,\eta^{2}} is the harmonic function on DD with boundary value 1η21_{\eta^{2}}. The above expression assumes that η1\eta^{1} is smooth, but one can check that ℰD​(η1,η2){\mathcal{E}}_{D}(\eta^{1},\eta^{2}) is a conformal invariant and hence can be defined for all domains. Also, ℰD​(η1,η2)=ℰD​(η2,η1){\mathcal{E}}_{D}(\eta^{1},\eta^{2})={\mathcal{E}}_{D}(\eta^{2},\eta^{1}). See [5], Chapter 5, for more details. When estimating excursion measures, we will use the following estimate that follows from the strong Markov property. Suppose η\eta is a crosscut of DD that separates η1\eta^{1} from η2\eta^{2}. Then

ℰD​(η1,η2)≤ℰD∖η​(η1,η)​supz∈ηϕ⁡(z).{\mathcal{E}}_{D}\bigl(\eta^{1},\eta^{2}\bigr)\leq{\mathcal{E}}_{D\setminus\eta}\bigl(\eta^{1},\eta\bigr)\sup_{z\in\eta}\phi(z). (9)

Lemma 2.5

There exists cc such that for all 0<u≤10<u\leq 1,

ℙ⁡{dist⁡[z,γ∞]<dist⁡[z,γσ]|γσ}≤c​eα⁡(u−λ)​r,{\mathbb{P}}\bigl\{\operatorname{dist}[z,\gamma_{\infty}]<\operatorname{dist}[z,\gamma_{\sigma}]|\gamma_{\sigma}\bigr\}\leq ce^{\alpha(u-\lambda)r},

where α=(4​a−1)/2>0\alpha=(4a-1)/2>0. In particular,

Let g:Hσ→ℍg\colon\;H_{\sigma}\rightarrow{\mathbb{H}} be a conformal transformation with g⁡(γ⁡(σ))=0g(\gamma(\sigma))=0, g⁡(∞)=∞g(\infty)=\infty. The curve η′=g∘lλ∗\eta^{\prime}=g\circ l^{*}_{\lambda} is a crosscut of ℍ{\mathbb{H}} contained in the bounded component of ℍ∖η{\mathbb{H}}\setminus\eta with positive endpoints x1≤x2x_{1}\leq x_{2}. Let us consider the conformal rectangle given by the component of ℍ∖(η∪η′){\mathbb{H}}\setminus(\eta\cup\eta^{\prime}) that contains both η\eta and η′\eta^{\prime} on its boundary and with η,η′\eta,\eta^{\prime} as two of the boundary arcs of the rectangle. The excursion measure between η\eta and η′\eta^{\prime} in this rectangle is the same as the excursion measure between lu∗l^{*}_{u} and lλ∗l_{\lambda}^{*} for the corresponding rectangle in Hσ∖(lu∗∪lλ∗)H_{\sigma}\setminus(l^{*}_{u}\cup l_{\lambda}^{*}). The Beurling estimate (see, e.g., [5], Theorem 3.76) implies that the latter is bounded above by ce−(λ−u)r/2ce^{-(\lambda-u)r/2}. Since η\eta separates η′\eta^{\prime} from the negative real line, we see that the excursion measure between η′\eta^{\prime} and (−∞,0](-\infty,0] in the unbounded component of ℍ∖η′{\mathbb{H}}\setminus\eta^{\prime} is bounded above by ce−(λ−u)r/2ce^{-(\lambda-u)r/2}. By standard estimates of the Poisson kernel in ℍ{\mathbb{H}}, this shows that diam(η′)≤ce−(λ−u)r/2x1\operatorname{diam}(\eta^{\prime})\leq ce^{-(\lambda-u)r/2}x_{1}, and hence by (7), the probability that an SLE\mathrm{SLE} path hits it is O(e−(λ−u)(4a−1)r/2)O(e^{-(\lambda-u)(4a-1)r/2}).

The next lemma strengthens (11) for κ≤4\kappa\leq 4. We do not know if it is true for 4<κ<84<\kappa<8. Let ℬ=ℬ1{\mathcal{B}}={\mathcal{B}}_{1} denote the disk of radius e−re^{-r} about zz.

Lemma 2.6

If κ≤4\kappa\leq 4, there exists cc such that if 0<u≤10<u\leq 1,

ℙ{γ[σ,∞)∩ℬ≠∅|γσ}≤ceα⁡(u−1)​r,{\mathbb{P}}\bigl\{\gamma[\sigma,\infty)\cap{\mathcal{B}}\neq\varnothing|\gamma_{\sigma}\bigr\}\leq ce^{\alpha(u-1)r}, (12)

As in the previous proof, we use (7) to see that

3.2 Natural length

By Theorem 3.1, with probability one we can define a function on 𝒬{\mathcal{Q}} by

μ⁡(Γ)=Contd⁡(γ∩Γ)=Contd⁡(γ∩int⁡(Γ))=Contd⁡(γ∩Γ¯).\mu(\Gamma)={\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(\gamma\cap\Gamma)={\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}\bigl(\gamma\cap{\operatorname{int}}(\Gamma)\bigr)={\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(\gamma\cap\overline{\Gamma}).
Proposition 3.3

On this event, μ\mu extends to be a Borel measure.

{proof}

For each Γ∈𝒬+\Gamma\in{\mathcal{Q}}^{+} and positive integer rr, we can define a Borel measure μr\mu_{r} by stating that the Radon–Nikodym derivative with respect to Lebesgue measure is Jr​(z)J_{r}(z). Since μr​(Γ)→μ​(Γ)\mu_{r}(\Gamma)\rightarrow\mu(\Gamma) and Γ\Gamma is compact, for each subsequence {rj}\{r_{j}\}, there is a sub-subsequence {rjk}\{r_{j_{k}}\} that converges to a measure μ′\mu^{\prime} with total mass μ⁡(Γ)\mu(\Gamma). By using a diagonalization argument, we can find a single sub-subsequence such that the convergence holds for all Γ∈𝒬+\Gamma\in{\mathcal{Q}}^{+}. By (22), we see that μ′​(∂Γ)=0\mu^{\prime}(\partial\Gamma)=0. Any open set UU can be written as a countable union of squares Γ∈𝒬+\Gamma\in{\mathcal{Q}}^{+} such that the interiors of the squares are disjoint. Hence, we can determine μ′​(U)\mu^{\prime}(U) for any open set, and hence we can see that m′=μm^{\prime}=\mu is unique.

We call μ\mu the (natural) occupation measure for the SLE\mathrm{SLE} curve γ\gamma. If DD is an open set, then we can find Dn∈𝒮ℍD_{n}\in{\mathcal{S}}_{\mathbb{H}} increasing to DD, and hence

𝔼⁡[μ⁡(D)]=∫DG⁡(z)​𝑑A​(z),𝔼⁡[μ​(D)2]=∫D×DG⁡(z,w)​𝑑A​(z)​𝑑A​(w).{\mathbb{E}}\bigl[\mu(D)\bigr]=\int_{D}G(z)\,dA(z),\qquad{\mathbb{E}}\bigl[\mu(D)^{2}\bigr]=\int_{D\times D}G(z,w)\,dA(z)\,dA(w).

∂nHs={z∈H¯s:dist⁡(z,∂Hs)≤2−n}.\partial_{n}H_{s}=\bigl\{z\in\overline{H}_{s}\colon\;\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial H_{s})\leq 2^{-n}\bigr\}.

Corollary 3.6

With probability one, if R<∞R<\infty, then for nn sufficiently large, Γ∈𝒬n\Gamma\in{\mathcal{Q}}_{n} with dist⁡(0,Γ)≤R\operatorname{dist}(0,\Gamma)\leq R,

By Chebyshev’s inequality, if Γ∈𝒬n\Gamma\in{\mathcal{Q}}_{n},

The result follows from the Borel–Cantelli lemma.

Note that

∂nℍ={z∈ℍ:ℑ⁡(z)≤2−n}.\partial_{n}{\mathbb{H}}=\bigl\{z\in{\mathbb{H}}\colon\;\Im(z)\leq 2^{-n}\bigr\}.

The next proposition establishes the Hölder continuity of the function t↦Contd(γ(0,t])t\mapsto{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}}(\gamma(0,t]) and completes the proof of (31).

Proposition 3.8

There exists α>0\alpha>0 such that with probability one for every t<∞t<\infty for all nn sufficiently large and all s≤ts\leq t,

It is known [3, 11] that for κ≠8\kappa\neq 8, the SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} curve is Hölder continuous with respect to the capacity parameterization. That is to say, there exists β=βκ>0\beta=\beta_{\kappa}>0 such that with probability one, if t<∞t<\infty, then for nn sufficiently large, and all 0≤s≤t0\leq s\leq t,

diam⁡(γ⁡[s,s+2−n])≤2−n​β.\operatorname{diam}\bigl(\gamma\bigl[s,s+2^{-n}\bigr]\bigr)\leq 2^{-n\beta}.

Let mm be the largest integer less than β​n\beta n. Then γ⁡[s,s+2−n]\gamma[s,s+2^{-n}] is contained in the union of four rectangles Γ1,…,Γ4∈𝒬m\Gamma_{1},\ldots,\Gamma_{4}\in{\mathcal{Q}}_{m}. For

nn sufficiently large, if Γj∈𝒬m+\Gamma_{j}\in{\mathcal{Q}}_{m}^{+}, then Corollary 3.6 implies that Contd+(Γj∩γ)≤m2−dm/2{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}^{+}}(\Gamma_{j}\cap\gamma)\leq m2^{-dm/2}. The result follows for α<β​d/2\alpha<\beta d/2.

limn→∞Contd+⁡[γ⁡[s+u,t]∩∂nHs]=0.\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}{\operatorname{Cont}_{d}^{+}}\bigl[\gamma[s+u,t]\cap\partial_{n}H_{s}\bigr]=0.

U=U0,k={x+iy:−2k≤x<2k,y≥1}.U=U_{0,k}=\bigl\{x+iy\colon\;-2^{k}\leq x<2^{k},y\geq 1\bigr\}.

This is what we will establish in this section.

4.2 One-point estimate

As is often the case, an important step in getting a two-point estimate is to get a sharp one-point estimate with good control on the error terms. Much of the necessary analysis has been done for SLE\mathrm{SLE}, and we review some of the methods here.

We will consider chordal SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} from 11 to w=e2​i​θw=e^{2i\theta} in the unit disk 𝔻{\mathbb{D}}, and we will study how close the path gets to the origin. We parameterize the SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} path γ\gamma using the radial parameterization. To be specific, we let DtD_{t} denote the component of 𝔻∖γt{\mathbb{D}}\setminus\gamma_{t} containing the origin and gt:Dt→𝔻g_{t}\colon\;D_{t}\rightarrow{\mathbb{D}} the unique conformal transformation with gt​(0)=0,gt​(γ⁡(t))=1g_{t}(0)=0,g_{t}(\gamma(t))=1. The radial parameterization is defined so that |gt′​(0)|=et|g_{t}^{\prime}(0)|=e^{t}. The total lifetime of the curve in this parameterization, TT, is finite with probability one. (If κ>4\kappa>4, TT is not the time that the curve reaches ww, but rather the time at which the curve disconnects the origin from ww. Although the SLE\mathrm{SLE} curves continues after this time, the domain DtD_{t} does not change so we do not need to consider the path after time TT.) We write wt=e2​i​θt=gt​(w)w_{t}=e^{2i\theta_{t}}=g_{t}(w). The path γt\gamma_{t}, and hence the transformations gtg_{t}, are determined by θs,0≤s≤t\theta_{s},0\leq s\leq t. If t>Tt>T, then gt=gTg_{t}=g_{T}. We let ℙθ,𝔼θ{\mathbb{P}}_{\theta},{\mathbb{E}}_{\theta} denote probabilities and expectations given by chordal SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} from 11 to e2​i​θe^{2i\theta}. The angle θt\theta_{t} satisfies a simple one-dimensional SDE. Its form is a little nicer if we consider a linear time change. If θ^t=θ2​a​t\hat{\theta}_{t}=\theta_{2at}, then θ^t\hat{\theta}_{t} satisfies the “radial Bessel equation”

dθ^t=(1−2a)cotθ^tdt+dBt,d\hat{\theta}_{t}=(1-2a)\cot\hat{\theta}_{t}\,dt+dB_{t},

where BtB_{t} is a standard Brownian motion. This equation is valid until the time T^=T/2​a\widehat{T}=T/2a at which θ^T^=θT∈{0,π}\hat{\theta}_{\widehat{T}}=\theta_{T}\in\{0,\pi\}.

The Koebe (1/4)(1/4)-theorem and Schwarz lemma implies that for 0≤t≤T0\leq t\leq T,

e−t−log⁡4≤dist⁡[0,γt]≤e−t.e^{-t-\log 4}\leq\operatorname{dist}[0,\gamma_{t}]\leq e^{-t}. (37)

Let St=SDt​(0,w,γ⁡(t))=S𝔻​(0,wt,1)=sin⁡θtS_{t}=S_{D_{t}}(0;w,\gamma(t))=S_{{\mathbb{D}}}(0;w_{t},1)=\sin\theta_{t}. Itô’s formula shows that

Mt=1{T>t}et⁡(2−d)St4​a−1M_{t}=1\{T>t\}e^{t(2-d)}S_{t}^{4a-1}

is a local martingale; more precisely, M^t=M2​a​t\widehat{M}_{t}=M_{2at} satisfies

d​M^t=(4​a−1)​[cot⁡θ^t]​M^t​d​Bt,t<T^.d\widehat{M}_{t}=(4a-1)[\cot\hat{\theta}_{t}]\widehat{M}_{t}\,dB_{t},\qquad t<\widehat{T}.

In fact, MtM_{t} is a continuous martingale with ℙ{MT=0}=1{\mathbb{P}}\{M_{T}=0\}=1.

Let 𝔻r{\mathbb{D}}_{r} denote the open disk of radius e−re^{-r} about the origin with closure 𝔻¯r\overline{\mathbb{D}}_{r}, and

τr=inf{t:dist⁡[0,γt]=e−r}=inf{t:γ⁡(t)∈𝔻¯r}.\tau_{r}=\inf\bigl\{t\colon\;\operatorname{dist}[0,\gamma_{t}]=e^{-r}\bigr\}=\inf\bigl\{t\colon\;\gamma(t)\in\overline{\mathbb{D}}_{r}\bigr\}.

r−2<r−log⁡4≤τr≤r.r-2<r-\log 4\leq\tau_{r}\leq r.

The measure obtained by tilting by the martingale MtM_{t} is called two-sided radial SLEκ\mathrm{SLE}_{\kappa} (from 00 to e2​i​θe^{2i\theta} in 𝔻{\mathbb{D}} going through the origin stopped when it reaches the origin). We will write ℙ∗,𝔼∗{\mathbb{P}}^{*},{\mathbb{E}}^{*} for probabilities and expectations with respect to this measure. These measures depend on the initial angle θ\theta and we will write ℙθ∗,𝔼θ∗{\mathbb{P}}^{*}_{\theta},{\mathbb{E}}^{*}_{\theta} if we wish to make this explicit. The quantity 𝔼θ∗{\mathbb{E}}^{*}_{\theta} is defined by saying that if XX is a random variable that depends only on γt\gamma_{t}, then

{remark*}

The same method shows that we can define nn-point Green’s function and we expect that

𝔼[Θ(D)n]=∫DnG(z1,…,zn)dA(z1)⋯dA(zn).{\mathbb{E}}\bigl[\Theta(D)^{n}\bigr]=\int_{D^{n}}G(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})\,dA(z_{1})\cdots dA(z_{n}).

At the moment, we cannot prove it because we have no upper bound for G⁡(z1,…,zn)G(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}).
